title: Coroner won't let jury rule police shooting a suicide: Police lawyer argues McMillan's death could be seen as self-inflicted
article: The coroner's jury examining the shooting death of Keldon McMillan could have ruled it a suicide, the lawyer representing city police argued as the hearing approached its conclusion Thursday.

"I think the option of suicide should have been left for the jury to consider," Barry Rossman told presiding coroner Doug Kovach after jurors left a Queen's Bench courtroom to begin their deliberations.

During his closing remarks to the jury, Kovach said homicide was the only conclusion open to them when deciding on the means of McMillan's death. In the context of a coroner's inquest, homicide does not imply wrongdoing. It simply means the death was caused by another human being, and not by accident, suicide, natural causes or undetermined means.
In some U.S. states, "suicide by police" is a legal category applicable to some deaths. Kovach overruled Rossman's objection, saying a suicide finding would not be supported by the evidence.
McMillan, 33, died in a field off Highway 41 about seven kilometres south of Wakaw on May 20, 2001, after leading city police and RCMP on a high-speed chase from his home in northeast Saskatoon.

His business was in financial jeopardy, his wife had just left him, and there was evidence he had ingested cocaine and alcohol shortly before the incident. Witnesses have testified he'd been talking about suicide for weeks, and had warned there would be a shootout if police were called.

The chase began just as officers were trying to surround McMillan's house to serve him with a temporary intervention order, a restraining order granted by a justice of the peace, obtained by his wife following a heated argument two days before.
After an RCMP spike belt flattened three of his tires, McMillan emerged from his truck with a handgun, disobeyed repeated police orders to drop it, then fired it into the air and walked away.

Seconds later, as a police dog ran to subdue him, he turned suddenly towards a group of officers with the gun raised. In the ensuing hail of gunfire, he shot and killed the dog before falling to the ground himself.
McMillan's father, Ralph McMillan, took the stand briefly to testify about their last conversation.

He went to his son's home for coffee that morning, and heard him make jokes about being a single man, he said. His son mentioned financial problems with his home-building business, but said he had other construction projects to work on until it was sorted out.

"I had no idea he was talking suicide or anything like that," McMillan told the jury. "As long as I was there, he was good." They did not discuss his marital problems much, and his son did not seem depressed, he added.
"If he had, I wouldn't have left."
Experts on police use of force testified Thursday the officers on the scene followed their training to the letter, and responded appropriately to the lethal threat McMillan posed at the moment.

The jury's main task was to make recommendations aimed at preventing a similar death in the future. Bruce Gibson, the lawyer representing the RCMP at the inquest, urged the jury to "try to make them practical," and to consider recommending that members of the public co-operate with police "so that violent situations do not occur."
Rossman did not have any suggestions to add on behalf of city police.
In the end, jurors adopted three recommendations posed by McMillan's family through their lawyer, Marty Minuk.

They suggested Saskatoon police add more RCMP radios to their cruisers, so that officers are not cut off from communications when pursuing a vehicle outside the city. The current system leaves most local police officers unable to contact their station by radio beyond Aberdeen.

That did not appear to be a problem during the McMillan chase, because the city's canine units also have RCMP radios. They were able to communicate with Saskatoon through RCMP dispatchers in Regina, and pass messages along to fellow officers.

The jury also recommended city police keep records of information given to officers during "parade" at the start of their shifts. Some of the officers sent to McMillan's home may have known less about the situation than others, but there is no way of confirming what they were told during parade that night, the inquest heard.

Jurors also recommended city police continue to study the idea of adding "tasers" -- devices used to temporarily paralyse suspects -- to their arsenal. The experts who testified Thursday said McMillan was too far away from police, and presented too much of an imminent threat, to make that option feasible.
McMillan's family declined comment throughout the inquest.
